query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn system was selected to reduce cost while retaining the mechanical performance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi; prior work reported comparable or better mechanical properties after excluding Co. Research on FeNiCrMn has mainly addressed corrosion, while studies of related high- and medium-entropy alloys examined dynamic responses under tension or compression, different temperatures and strain rates, compositional changes, and the presence of cracks or voids. Those studies established that dynamic properties are sensitive to loading regime and material condition, but their different chemistries and defect states do not identify what governs FeNiCrMn. Under the constraints of retaining the Co-free composition and its strength–ductility balance, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains the dynamic behavior of solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes? Define a controlled study capable of testing the hypothesis, its applicable boundaries, the prior findings that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In solidified Co‐free FeNiCrMn, the dynamic mechanical response across temperature and strain rate regimes is governed by a competition between conventional dislocation glide and a transformation‐induced plasticity (TRIP) mechanism mediated by deformation-induced stacking faults. Under higher strain rates and lower temperatures, limited dislocation mobility promotes dislocation pile-ups that trigger stacking fault formation, initiating a TRIP effect that enhances strain hardening while preserving the balance between strength and ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast, solidified Co‐free FeNiCrMn alloy with a primarily fcc microstructure that is metastable with respect to stacking fault and phase transformation mechanisms.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled mechanical deformation via tensile or compressive tests at a series of strain rates (from quasi-static ~10^−3 s^−1 to dynamic ~10^3 s^−1) and temperatures (room temperature to cryogenic conditions) without altering the base alloy chemistry.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted under well-controlled strain rates and temperature conditions ensuring minimal variation in microstructural state other than that induced by deformation.
generation.structural_mediator: Deformation-induced stacking faults that serve as nucleation sites for TRIP within the fcc matrix.
generation.mechanism: At elevated strain rates and lower temperatures, reduced dislocation mobility leads to their accumulation and pile-up, increasing local stresses that initiate stacking fault formation. These faults catalyze a transformation-led plasticity process (TRIP), which enhances strain hardening and offsets ductility losses usually associated with high strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: A shift in mechanical behavior where, under high strain rate and low temperature conditions, the alloy exhibits a higher flow stress and a more pronounced work-hardening rate compared to baseline moderate conditions, without compromising overall ductility due to the TRIP contribution.
generation.baseline: Mechanical tests at moderate strain rates (around 10^−3 s^−1) and room temperature, where dislocation glide dominates and stacking fault induced TRIP mechanisms are minimally active.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies primarily to as-cast FeNiCrMn alloys with minimal prior thermomechanical processing; post-processing routes that significantly alter stacking fault energy or phase stability may fall outside the predictive scope of this mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative interplay between dislocation glide and TRIP contributions under varying conditions remains to be fully delineated. In particular, the threshold conditions for appreciable stacking fault activation and its sensitivity to slight microstructural variations introduce uncertainty.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare as-cast FeNiCrMn specimens and subject them to a series of mechanical tests (tensile and/or compressive) under systematically varied strain rates (quasi-static to dynamic) and temperature conditions (room temperature vs. cryogenic). Utilize in-situ and post-deformation TEM to quantitatively assess dislocation arrangements and stacking fault densities along with standard stress-strain measurements.
measurements: Stress-strain curves to determine flow stress and work-hardening rates across conditions
TEM imaging to quantify stacking fault density and observe any phase transformation (TRIP) features
Comparative analysis of microstructural evolution at different test conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If increasing strain rate or reducing temperature does not produce a statistically significant increase in stacking fault density and a corresponding increase in flow stress and work-hardening rate (relative to the baseline moderate condition), or if alternative mechanisms dominate the behavior, then the proposed mechanism is falsified.

Effects of V Addition on the Deformation Mechanism and Mechanical Properties of Non-Equiatomic CoCrNi Medium-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: Equiatomic CoCrNi medium-entropy alloys exhibit superior strength and ductility. In this work, a non-equiatomic CoCrNi alloy with low stacking fault energy was designed, and different fractions of V were added to control the stacking fault energy and lattice distortion. Mechanical properties were evaluated by tensile tests, and deformation microstructures were characterized by transmission electron microscope (TEM). The main deformation mechanisms of CoCrNiV alloy with low V content are dislocation slip, stacking faults, and deformation-induced HCP phase transformation, while the dominant deformation patterns of CoCrNiV alloy with high V contents are dislocation slip and stacking faults. The yield strength increases dramatically when the V content is high, and the strain-hardening behavior changes non-monotonically with increasing the V content. V addition increases the stacking fault energy (SFE) and lattice distortion. The lower strain-hardening rate of 6V alloy than that of 2V alloy is dominated by the SFE. Influence of ordered L12 precipitation on strain-rate dependent mechanical behavior in a eutectic high entropy alloy

Abstract: Recent studies indicate that eutectic high-entropy alloys can simultaneously possess high strength and high ductility, which have potential industrial applications. The present study focuses on Al0.7CoCrFeNi, a lamellar dual-phase (fcc + B2) precipitation-strengthenable eutectic high entropy alloy. This alloy exhibits an fcc + B2 (B2 with bcc nano-precipitates) microstructure resulting in a combination of the soft and ductile fcc phase together with hard B2 phase. Low temperature annealing leads to the precipitation of ordered L12 intermetallic precipitates within the fcc resulting in enhanced strength. The strengthening contribution due to fine scale L12 is modeled using Orowan dislocation bowing and by-pass mechanism. The alloy was tested under quasi-static (strain-rate = 10−3 s−1) tensile loading and dynamic (strain-rate = 103 s−1) compressive loading. Nanoindentation behavior of high entropy alloys with transformation-induced plasticity

Abstract: Nanoindentation of three metastable dual-phase high entropy alloys (HEAs) was performed to obtain their inherent elastoplastic deformation responses. Excellent combination of hardness and elastic modulus in as-cast condition confirmed that, their inherently higher strength compared to other HEAs reported in literature, can be attributed to alloy chemistry induced phase stability. Further, hardness of 8.28 GPa combined with modulus of 221.8 GPa was obtained in Fe-Mn-Co-Cr-Si-Cu HEA by annealing the as-cast material, which is the best hardness-modulus combination obtained to date in HEAs from nanoindentation.
